analysis.one_liner: Repeals oil company tax breaks and sends families a one-time gas-price rebate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a long list of special tax breaks for oil and gas companies, including deductions for drilling costs, credits for marginal and enhanced-recovery wells, and favorable accounting methods for the biggest integrated oil companies. It would also clarify that oil from tar sands and oil shale is taxed under the federal petroleum excise tax, which funds oil spill cleanup. The revenue side pairs with a one-time rebate: $500 per taxpayer ($1,000 for couples) plus $500 per dependent age 16 or older, tied to 2022 gas prices. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers would receive a one-time refundable rebate of $500 ($1,000 for joint filers), plus $500 for each dependent age 16 or older, paid even to households that owe little or no federal income tax [S3]. Taxpayers generally would benefit if the money raised by ending oil company tax breaks funds the rebate rather than adding to deficits. The oil spill excise tax fix would also put tar sands and oil shale under the tax that finances spill cleanup, spreading that cost to those fuels [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Families would get a one-time rebate of $500 per taxpayer ($1,000 on a joint return) plus $500 per dependent age 16 or older, credited for their first tax year beginning in 2022 [S3].

The rebate is fully refundable, meaning households that owe little or no income tax still receive the money, and the bill directs the Treasury to run outreach so eligible people learn they can claim it [S3].

The bill repeals a series of tax provisions that benefit oil and gas producers, including the marginal well credit, the enhanced oil recovery credit, immediate expensing of intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, and the deduction for tertiary injectants, effective for tax years after 2022 [S3].

The largest integrated oil companies (over 500,000 barrels of daily crude production and over $1 billion in gross receipts) would be barred from using LIFO inventory accounting, which can defer taxable income when prices rise [S3].
The bill expands the crude oil excise tax so it covers oil from tar sands and oil shale, revenue that feeds the trust fund that pays for oil spill cleanup [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose the tax breaks the bill repeals, including drilling-cost expensing, percentage depletion, and LIFO accounting for the largest integrated firms, and would face higher taxable income as a result [S3]. Some of that cost could be passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices for fuel, and smaller producers of marginal wells would lose credits that specifically support low-output wells [S3].

drawbacks.text: Repealing tax benefits for production, such as immediate expensing of drilling costs and credits for marginal wells, could raise production costs that companies pass through as higher fuel prices for consumers [S3].

The rebate is one-time and retroactive to 2022, so it compensates for gas prices that were already paid rather than providing ongoing relief, and its advance-payment mechanics reference 2020 and 2021 filing years in ways that add administrative complexity [S3].
The marginal well credit the bill repeals was designed to keep low-output wells viable; eliminating it could speed the retirement of those wells and affect jobs in oil-producing regions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a direct, refundable payment to households with the repeal of long-standing tax breaks for a single industry, so the money for the rebate comes from the companies losing the breaks. The main honest objection is that some of the tax increase on producers could surface as higher fuel prices, partly offsetting the rebate, and the one-time rebate addresses past prices rather than future ones. The design is straightforward, but its narrow base of four sponsors meant it had no realistic path even if the design held up.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Sean Casten introduced the People Over Petroleum Act in the House on March 23, 2023, joined by Representatives Blumenauer, Levin, and McClellan [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, which is the standard first step for tax legislation [S2].

The complete action history shows only two actions: introduction and the committee referral. No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
The bill attracted 3 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no Republican support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the tax breaks the bill would have repealed, and the biggest integrated firms kept LIFO accounting, because the bill never advanced. Households never received the one-time rebate.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and all 3 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the committee that buried the bill was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill repeals a set of tax benefits specific to the industry, including drilling-cost expensing, percentage depletion, the marginal well and enhanced oil recovery credits, and the passive-loss exception for working interests [S3]. The industry's interest in keeping these breaks runs against taxpayers who would otherwise fund the rebate from general revenue or forego it [S3].

These firms (over 500,000 barrels daily production, over $1 billion in receipts) would lose LIFO inventory accounting and face curtailed foreign tax credits for payments to countries where they receive specific economic benefits, both of which can defer or reduce their taxes [S3]. Their losses under the bill are the bill's revenue.

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale producers
industries.note: The bill makes oil derived from tar sands and oil shale subject to the federal petroleum excise tax that funds oil spill cleanup, an adjustment that treats these fuels like conventional crude [S3]. This aligns the producers' tax treatment with the public's interest in having spill-cleanup costs financed by the fuels that pose the risk.
